utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 26th of June, 2007. My greetings to the Prosecution, to the Defence counsel, and to the accused, as well as to all the people in and around the courtroom. First of all there is a problem with our timetable. There was a request by Mr. Karnavas yesterday regarding the 15th of August. We discussed the matter this morning, and we believe that it would be possible to have the three days of hearing as scheduled as of the 16th of August in the morning. We could have the 16th in the afternoon, and the Friday, 17th of August or the afternoon if need be. So there it is. It will make it possible for everybody to come back peacefully and to be able to start after the recess on the 16th of August. Secondly, we're going to issue a decision. It is, rather, a reminder by the Trial Chamber regarding the way guideline 6 should be interpreted. It deals with the admission of documents not adduced in court. At its hearing of the 25th of June, 2007 -- at the hearing, sorry, Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Alaburic raised a problem as to the way to interpret guideline number 6 as stated in the decision of the 13th of July, 2006, regarding the admission of evidence. Mr. Karnavas asked the Chamber to reconsider whether it would be possible for the Defence to seek admission of evidence under the said guideline, among other reasons because there are, as alleged, time constraints during the hearing. Ms. Alaburic also argued at the hearing of the 6th of November, 2006, that I amended the said guideline by allowing the Defence, as it is allowed to the Prosecution, to seek admission by way of written motion meeting the criteria of the guideline. The Trial Chamber recalls, first of all, that guideline 6 of the decision of the 13th of July, 2006, provides that the -- only the Prosecution can seize the Trial Chamber of a written motion for the admission of evidence which were not put before the witness in court. Then after saying that it was willing to somewhat loosen up the conditions stated out in guideline 6, the Trial Chamber heard the submissions of parties at the hearing of 6 November 2006, including their proposal to amend the guideline in order to allow not only the Prosecution but also the Defence to file written motions for admission of evidence not put to a witness in court. Following the submissions the Trial Chamber issued, on the 29th of November, 2006, a decision amending the decision of the 13th of July, 2006. In its decision of the 29th of November, 2006, the Trial Chamber very clearly stated that: "At the state of the trial, namely during the Prosecution case, the possibility to file written motions before the Chamber under guideline 6 is only opened to the Prosecution." Finally, by way of a confidential decision of the 24th of May, 2007, on the request by the Praljak Defence for admission of two documents as evidence, the Trial Chamber once again reminded the parties that guideline 6 could only be used by the Prosecution. With regard to the intervention of the Presiding Judge during the hearing of the 6th of November, 2006, it had to be seen within the context of submissions by the parties following a proposal by the Trial Chamber to loosen the conditions stated in the guideline. At any rate, this intervention was made prior to the decision of the 29th of November, 2006, and can therefore in no way be interpreted as challenging or questioning the written decision of the 29th of November, 2006. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber maintains its position, namely that at the state of the trial it is not for the Defence to request by way of written motion for the Chamber to admit evidence which was not put before a witness in court. The Defence will be able and allowed, if need be, when it comes to the Defence case to seize the Chamber of such motions in similar conditions to the conditions applying to the Prosecution. So in a nutshell, the Trial Chamber only allows the Prosecution to file written motions regarding documents that were not submitted to a witness, and the Defence equally will be put in a similar situation and will be given the same possibility when we start with the Defence case. The Prosecution then will not be allowed to request by way of written motion for documents to be admitted. This being said, regarding the Defence motion for reconsideration by the Trial Chamber of the time period allotted to the Defence for the cross-examination of the present witness, the Trial Chamber maintains its position. The Defence will be given six hours. Should there be new elements transpiring on cross-examination that justify more flexibility, the Trial Chamber might possibly, depending on the time remaining, grant an extension of this time, but only so if it's deemed relevant depending on the questions dealt with. Finally, I'd like to tell the parties that the Trial Chamber filed a written decision today regarding the proceedings under Rule 65 [as interpreted] ter. I do invite you to read the decision, and there is also an individual opinion by myself. Let us have the witness brought in, the examination-in-chief to be continued. Mr. Kruger, you have 1 hour and 120 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minor correction. On line 13, page 4, do not read 65 but 92. Good afternoon, sir. We are going to resume with the examination if chief. And, Mr. Kruger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have no German translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now in German?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Colonel, yesterday evening we concluded with looking at Exhibit -- you don't need to turn to it now, Exhibit 03470.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I could perhaps have the assistance of the usher to provide the exhibit binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in that document the very last thing we looked at yesterday was a passage which stated that HV troops, special forces from the 41st HV Brigade from Split are carrying a counter-attack in Buna, Bacevici and this was written on the 15th of July, 1993. Would I like to move on from this point and look at the next document related to what -- to the previous document, and this is Exhibit 3494. Exhibit 3494. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this is an ECMM report. Sorry. No, it's not an ECMM report. It comes from the European Community Liaison Officer in Kiseljak, and it's the daily information summary for 16 July 1993. Once again, would you have seen or received this report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we got them as a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can once again turn to paragraph 6 of this report entitled "SpaBat sector." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph (A), which deals with Mostar, we see under the first bullet: "Fighting between the HVO and BiH continued to the south of Mostar in the Buna Bacevic areas." And then it goes on: "After the HVO and HVO troops launched a counter-attack on the morning of 15 July." And if we go to the fourth bullet, paragraph 4 on that page: "Fresh Croat soldiers have been seen in Mostar ..." And two lines down: "Significantly, these soldiers appear to be unfamiliar with the names of the surrounding villages." Can you comment on these two portions, add anything to what's already stated here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish to -- I didn't object yesterday, but now we're going a gentleman to comment about a passage without laying a foundation, and think I we need to lay a foundation before -- you know, was this his observation, and if he says yes then he can comment, but here someone is giving a value judgement such as it appears that they didn't know, they were unfamiliar with the surroundings. So I just think that, first, was he aware, keeping in mind where he was located at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the issues mentioned in this paragraph, first of all the question of HV troops being present at this period in time in the region of Mostar, was that something which the ECMM had also been aware of or was discussing looking at at that stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this together amongst ourselves again and again within ECMM. My CC had no concrete indications of HV troops. We didn't see any personally, and there were certain cases of suspicion, but we didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell the Court in what way were -- was the ECMM able to investigate or look for the presence of HV troops? And at what times during the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me again, Your Honour. I hate being a pest but I am going to be critical at this point. First, it assumes that there was an investigation. I think the question should be, you know, what, if anything, did he do. We know that he doesn't know anything personally. He didn't see anything. So now the question is if he wants to go about it in a roundabout way, was there an investigation, yes, and it may be based on an investigation he might be able to comment, even though he doesn't have firsthand knowledge, but I think it assumes a fact that's not in evidence yet, and it may never be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, please let us try to avoid interventions by Mr. Karnavas. It might be time-consuming, but he wants to comply with the proceedings. So try to comply yourself by putting questions that are such that there is no such objection. It's not of interest to me because I'm interested in what there is in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, a recurring theme in the documents that we have seen up to now, and it will also appear from a few of the documents which we will still look at, are reports that, especially from the ECMM side, there are allegations of the presentation of HV troops, but you have not seen any evidence of that personally or your ECMM monitors. Could you comment or tell the Court how the Court should view this information as -- does this mean that there were no HV troops as far as you're concerned or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, this did not come from ECMM but from the other side. There was a general mandate from the EC Mostar to monitor border to Croatia, to see if HV troops had crossed the border. And then round about the 13th of June, after these events had happened, there was a special order to repeat this and to intensify our efforts, so that for some days a team checked the border with Croatia several times, but during the day. This could only be visual inspection, travelling up and down, and sometimes an attempt was made to see if there were any tracks in the area. It was a mountainous area, and so it was difficult to see traces. And during these checks we did not find any indications of any HV troops. The only time where we had suspicion, but I cannot confirm this that it was a case of HV troops, in Siroki Brijeg one morning, very early we were in our premises and there were artillery shots, and we saw two artillery stations close to Siroki Brijeg. We assumed that these shots were aimed around the area of Breznice Vjadi [phoen], but it was an assumption. That's all I can say. These -- there were two other posts in other areas. These could have been the same ones, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just for clarity, you mentioned that -- sorry, I'm looking for it in the transcript. Ah. And then you said and then around the 13th of June, after these events had happened. Is that correct, the 13th of June, or are you referring to July?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. It was -- perhaps I made a mistake. It was July when these events to the north of Mostar and the south took place. 30th of July, it was afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we can move to another exhibit, and this is Exhibit 3511. Exhibit 3511. You have it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is once again a report or a daily information summary from the European Community Liaison Officer for the 17th of July, 1993. Would you have had, received this document as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume I did, because we got all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn once again to the sixth paragraph of the document. Do you have that, paragraph 6, "SpaBat sector."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Paragraph (A) is once again "Mostar" and if we look at the end of the bullets or after the bullets, "Comment", in the first bullet under "Comment": "There have been further confirmed reports of HV troops in the area." Were you -- did you receive any further information since the previous report regarding this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no personal knowledge over the events that I have already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the third bullet, the very last line on that page: "Movement of UNPROFOR vehicles in the area of Mostar, Capljina is still being prevented by the HVO." What was the situation with regard to the ECMM in these areas?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Capljina, yes. Of course, we were still of course prevented from go into Mostar, not Capljina. And as I said yesterday, in the area of Capljina, Medjugorje, Ceduk [as interpreted], only one time, it was one day or two, I don't know exactly, there was a street barrier. We were prevented from crossing certain crossroads and we were diverted into another direction. Otherwise, for us in Capljina there was no particular restriction, and no one of my team had reported any such restrictions either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, just for the record, you mentioned on page 10, line 8, a place called Ceduk. Is that correct? You mentioned three places, Capljina, Medjugorje, and in the -- and in the record, it came out the third place as Ceduk. I'm just checking whether that's --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry. I think I was only describing the area in general, that is, Capljina, Citluk, because it all belongs together, and of course there are other areas I could mention to the south. But this was the entire area we covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's cleared it up. If we can move to the next exhibit in the binder. That's Exhibit 3554. Exhibit 3554. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also have is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a report, a daily report for 20 July, and it's an ECMM report from Brad and Peter. Are you aware of this report? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in the section which says "Political situation," -- so, no, the next paragraph, "Military situation": "Restrictions to movement continue. We were stopped by a police patrol on the north side of Citluk." My first question is: The reference to a police patrol, do you know which police this refers to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this, it's reported in the same paragraph that the police told the monitors that they should follow the agreement made with UNPROFOR, and then there's a comment. "Neither we nor UNPROFOR know anything about an agreement. End comment." Can you tell the Court about that? Was there such an agreement that you knew of or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would have been an agreement against our own possibilities of movement, and this is an agreement that I think can be excluded. This report presumably refers to what I said. Citluk is not far from Medjugorje, and this was this crossroads that I mentioned before, the one that the team refers to in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 4 of -- of this report. "Humanitarian situation." "At the coordination meeting UNHCR described urgent problem involving the movement of Muslim detainees and refugees. Last Saturday they were asked by the HVO government to establish a transit camp in Ljubuski for up to 10.000 persons..." And then two lines further: "UNHCR refused this as it would be aiding ethnic cleansing." Were you aware of this incident or what's reported in this paragraph and, if so, can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not involved in this, so to that extent I cannot comment on it. However, I had heard - I cannot confirm this - that the wagon camp in Ljubuski -- not Ljubuski, in Capljina, possibly was kind of transit camp and had been used as such, but I don't know that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Following on on this, perhaps if we can just look at the final paragraph, paragraph -- penultimate paragraph, paragraph 8, the assessment. "The international community is being pressured into aiding in ethnic cleansing. If they do not help, they are accused of letting people starve. Pressure must be brought to bear on those responsible for the mass relocations." Can you comment on this assessment, what it implies or what it means?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in particular, as I said yesterday, the International Committee of the Red Cross was always in a cleft stick. They wanted to help and had to help on one hand. On the other hand they were faced with the criticism if they did help, then they would help with expulsion or ethnic cleansing of the refugees. And this was the permanent atmosphere, and it was a constant concern of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's look at the next exhibit, 3611. Exhibit 3611. Do you have the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also have this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is an ECMM daily summary report for 21 July 1993, and it's -- at the end, it's signed, "Regards, Jacques Witgen, senior ops-officer." Do you know of this report? Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I presume that I received it. In fact, I'm sure I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Jacques Witgen, who was he, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get to know him as far as I'm aware, because from Zenica we were very far removed. You have to imagine the mountains involved, an eight-hour journey. So they were very rarely in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at section 2 or paragraph 2 of this document on the first page: "CC Mostar area of responsibility." And if we look at the second paragraph under that section, it says: "A meeting was arranged today with Mr. Petkovic to try to arrange for the problem of exchange of prisoners ..." Two lines down: "But he didn't come and had HCC was told by phone that the responsibility of those matters was now in the hands of the deputy chief of police, Mr. Pusic." Can you tell the Court about that incident or about this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact this did not take place, and we were not in a position because of a lack of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... President. Your Honours, I want to raise an objection. My learned friend is now obviously stating something that is not even in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief. It was never alleged that Mr. Pusic was the deputy chief of police. It's not in the indictment. It's not in the pre-trial brief. If you look at the date, the 21st of July, 1993, if you look at paragraph 13 of the pre-trial brief, it is obvious, at least based on what the Prosecutor says, Mr. Pusic was in a different position as of the 5th of July that year, entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. The -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution is simply putting the document to the witness and is restating exactly what is stated in the document for the witness's comment, and one of the aspects which we could touch upon, if the witness knows, is the title accorded to Mr. Pusic. If I may continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, can you comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President. The same sort of question was asked yesterday of this witness and the witness said he didn't understand at all what Mr. Pusic's job was exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He might tell us that he doesn't know exactly. Please put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you have heard the discussion. In the last line of the quoted section there's reference to the "deputy chief of police, Mr. Pusic." Now, you had met Mr. Pusic. Did you know exactly what his title was, or position?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was under the impression, and this was confirmed in 1994 when I heard the name again, that the area of responsibility of Mr. Pusic was not clearly defined from -- I myself didn't quite understand the definition. So he was responsible for displaced persons, then refugees. That's what I heard as well, I seem to remember. And in 1994 he said he was also responsible for prisoners of war. Hence it was never quite clear to me. That's what I stated yesterday about wording here, on the one hand I assume of course that this was said by the mayor of Siroki Brijeg. Otherwise, it wouldn't say so here. I don't think because of the unclear definition of his area of responsibility that I've just described a completely new term is being used. That is not probable. That would really not be good work. That would not really be careful -- careful work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Are you able to provide the Court with further insight as to why the meeting with Mr. Petkovic was cancelled? Can you recall any reasons being given?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. I don't know that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did or was contact taken up with Mr. Pusic regarding the matters for the exchange -- or the problem of exchange of prisoners in this case, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to establish communications, and it didn't work out. I think that the attempt was made. Our major line of communication was the -- the secretary of Mr. Stojic, and I can remember the name of Franceska, but this was the only acceptable link of communication that we still had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now that you mentioned her, can you tell the Court who was Franceska?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the office of Minister Stojic via which we also tried to establish other contacts. But as I said, the links of communication were quite difficult because of technical possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who was Franceska specifically?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was his -- she was the secretary that the -- the lady in the secretariat. She was responsible for the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look at -- under -- on this the document paragraph 2, "CC Mostar." The first paragraph under that section. It says: "HCC met today ..." First question, does that refer to you, still, as HCC?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I linguistically intervene, Mr. Kruger. The translation says she was the secretary, but vorzimmerdame is not really secretary. It would rather be the lady at the reception desk. Would you agree with that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was not the lady in the reception. She was the secretary who was in -- who was responsible and who also turned us away, to say it quite clearly, that was also manning her area of responsibility. So she was not the lady in reception. I think it's nuances. She was really in charge for Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's worthwhile just lingering on this point for a while longer. You say she was responsible, "who also turned us away, to say it quite clearly." Can you tell the Court what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to illustrate this by using an example. We have made lots of attempts to get to the minister, to the minister of defence and his deputy, and then every day we were told, for example, "Today he is absent. He is not here. He will only be here at 5.00." But then we tried at 5.00 and he wasn't there. "You can try tomorrow." She told us, "Yes, I saw him, but he's gone away again." So the quite obvious behaviour that we know from such places, from secretariats. But it could be like that but it could have been different on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let's turn then to that paragraph, the first page of the document, section 2, "CC Mostar." Do you have that? And then the first paragraph of that section. "HCC met today..." My question was, HCC, was that still you at this stage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was still me, because the transfer to my successor, the hand-over hadn't happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It says then: You "met today the mayor of Siroki Brijeg, who told that they were evacuating Muslims to Croatia, 'Because there was no other solution.'" Can you comment on that or tell the Court what this was about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Siroki Brijeg there were only very few Muslim refugees, and he said it in general terms, and he was also referring to other areas, to other cities, because he basically knew about this activity. He -- he might have talked about it possibly as well in order to make it clear that we were talk -- in his view it was an evacuation, a peaceful movement of population and nothing else. So that might have been the intention behind this. He didn't specify that either. He didn't give any figures. Of course the question was asked again, and then things were not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The very next line it says: "Nevertheless, most of about 7.000 displaced persons in the town are Croats who stay there." Can you comment on this in light of what was just said about the Muslims being evacuated, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number of Croat refugees in Siroki Brijeg I heard about occasionally. They were mainly Croats who had been accepted in guest families. So they came from the East Herzegovina but also from Jajce where in winter the march started of refugees from Jajce. There were probably also temporary -- there was also a temporary accommodation, but the main share had been -- were staying with guest families, with host families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Colonel, if we turn the page, just one last thing on this document. Just before the third section, the paragraph above, the last sentence reads: "The team around for a meeting with the HVO Brigade commander in Domanovici. If it succeeds, it will be the first time since long that ECMM goes so close to Mostar." To your recollection, did -- was this successful that the ECMM could then -- or that team could then go to Mostar or close to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember in my time there were only a few days left that it was -- that it didn't happen, but I would really have to check it in another document and read up on it again, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn two documents further, Exhibit 3674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, let's stay with this particular exhibit, and I'd like us to go back to item two, paragraph 2. Here when reading this text the way it was drafted, we get the impression that there was a meeting organised on that particular day with Mr. Petkovic in order to try to arrange the problem of exchange of prisoners and, in particular, the situation of the Tuzla delegation. Let's proceed with -- when we read the rest of the text, we see that apparently Petkovic never showed up, and then he we read: "HCC," that is to say you, "heard on the phone that the responsibility of those matters was now in the hands of the deputy chief of police, Mr. Pusic." So apparently Mr. Petkovic did not show up, so you called someone on the phone, and that someone told to you that these matters fell under the competence of Mr. Pusic, but do you remember that particular point or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recollect how it technically happened. The most probable is that on the return to CC I got on the phone, or one of my monitors phoned, and that it happened after the mayor of the Siroki Brijeg had left, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to Exhibit 3674. Exhibit 3674. You have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document is dated the -- it's the weekly summary for 23 July, and it says at the end: "Best regards, HCC Mostar." Was this a report drafted by you or written by you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that it's from me. It might also have been Sir Martin Garrod who worded it, but then in conjunctions we cooperated. It was a document from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look under (A), the "Weekly assessment," the very first part. "Because our current inability to observe and report on key parts of our area first-hand, our assessment has to be our best interpretation of current events." Can you tell the Court what that means?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to read that passage again. That's Sir Martin Garrod's English. I recognised it. Yes. What it means is that we got immediate information about what happened. We were very remote of that. We were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What were the sources of your information?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the observer officers of the United Nations, the Spanish Battalion, and contacts of the UNHCR or International Red Cross, and also the man in the street, but less so or not at all a real insight into the area of contacts with officers -- with officials, or contacts who were close to the front line. We did have the contact with the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at Section (B), the "Weekly projection" toward the end, the first line says: "We will be pursuing the freedom of movement question this week ..." With whom would that have been pursued?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was supposed to be made clear with our joint visit of my successor and myself in Zenica so that at the higher level than ours we could look into that matter again. In the meantime, we had an incident that a Mercedes had been stolen, and internally that also created, too, a restriction of movement. We could not operate so easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, if you say, "We will be pursuing the freedom of movement question this week," does that mean that you would be taking it up with the office RC Zenica or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm correct as far as the dates are concerned. I think afterwards I went with Sir Martin Garrod to Zenica, also to organise the hand-over, and the paragraph under (B) alludes to that and makes it clear that we're going to go to Zenica and with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look two paragraphs above that. This is the paragraph which reads: "There are increasing signs." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The second sentence, that's the last word of the third line: "They also seem to be appreciating that the world press is heavily critical of their treatment to date of their major displaced persons problem, and we would see a more moderate and humane line developing, an indication being the statement of Mr. Pogarcic yesterday, the journalists and the United States military attache had been permitted to visit the Heliodrom." Do you recall this or do you know what this relates to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also a visit with Sir Martin Garrod and myself to Mr. Pogarcic in the days prior to that date. And I think in that context I seem to remember he also talked about the visit of the Heliodrom. So we included this in the report. But what happened in the end, what was the outcome, I cannot tell you. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, a final aspect on this -- on this document, and we may actually have dealt with this aspect about 15 minutes ago, but if we look at just the paragraph above the one we were dealing with now, it says: "Although there can be no doubt that there are elements of HV troops in Herzegovina, we ourselves have observed very little in the way of formed bodies ...," et cetera. My only question here is that first part, "Although there can be no doubt." Can you tell the Court on what basis that was written?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken from the frequent reports from Kiseljak in order to shortly summarise it in a form and transmit it to RC Zenica. And the fact that we ourselves observed very little really -- we have observed nothing, I would like to stick to that even though it might sound differently when you read this here. This was our interpretation after seeing the guns in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to Exhibit 3710. Exhibit 3710. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document with your name at the top, Klaus Nissen, HCC Mostar, and then July 26, 1993, although at the right of the page there's a date 30 July 1993. First of all, do you recognise or know of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a personal report to the German head of delegation in Mostar, and at the same time a manuscript or -- which was written subsequent to a presentation in Zagreb. It was a kind of debriefing document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document relates, of course, to the involvement of HV troops in Southern Bosnia. And if we look at the first paragraph, about halfway down, there's a portion which says: "The value of such an assessment may be limited, because we were not allowed to work in the darkness, but we did not observe any traces in the terrain, which we as soldiers should have been able to interpret." Is this what you were referring to earlier this afternoon when we spoke about this matter of observing HV troops?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to this in this particular document, which is dated later, the end of July. Again, I summarised what seemed to me to be important to report to the ECMM of Chief of Operations in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look at Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, one clarification. This document, 3710, is addressed to the head of the German delegation you said in Mostar. Yesterday, I also realised on examining Exhibit 3807, that you also sent a report to the German delegation in Zagreb regarding the issue of the three interpreters that had been captured. The three interpreters and a driver had been captured by the HVO; what is this German delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zagreb, Your Honour, there was a sort of ambassador who was in Zagreb representing the German national side at the ECMM. He looked after the monitors, the reports. He wrote his own comments for the Foreign Ministry, and for Federal Minister Kinkel. And it was not desired to use national channels, but I must say that each nation did have to its own national delegations, now and again when it seemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, one final document on HV presence if we can turn to Exhibit 2643. Exhibit 2643. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document from Brad or signed by Brad. It's dated the 5th of June, 1993, and it's an ECMM team report, and this is the report which at the -- in paragraph 8 refers to a search of the Bosnian navy, and nothing was found. Do you recall this document or had you seen it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We note in paragraph 8 once again this was just an early report of: "Some evidence has been seen suggesting possible HV presence in the area ..." I won't ask you further on this, but perhaps just three lines -- or two lines below that. "Team patrol the southern extremes of Bosnia in search of the Bosnian navy. Nothing was found." Can you perhaps just tell the Court what that was or what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I apologise to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be proper, if the Prosecution is showing the document like this, and we'll deal with it during the cross-examination of course, but it would be proper for him to read out everything, the one or two sentences in between. That would be the right thing to do. And it says: "The possible presence -- suggesting possible HV presence in the area," and it says, "Confirmation still not required. Team will continue to pursue the matter." So the correct way of going about this would be to read all the sentences in between as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. I will try and assist in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For this document, though, I think we've dealt with these matters sufficiently at this stage, and I would just like to ask still about the navy and what that meant or what that was about.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this is a joke, but where is the joke? There was a certain frustration in the teams to be asked again and again about the HV troops and to be unable to come up with an answer, the result being that they said, "Then ask us about the navy." It was roughly like this. Which we couldn't find either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, a final question on the access to Mostar question -- or matter. Did you personally try to gain access via alternative routes during your time with CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question? Do you mean the entire time I was there when we didn't have access, in June, for example, or July? Over the entire period of time, not only the last period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps only the last period when access was restricted, and if you have a specific example. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of June I made a large detour with the French driver without an interpreter not to endanger the interpreter, and we didn't have an armoured vehicle, we made a great detour coming from the south towards Mostar. This was in June. And to our great surprise, because we had assumed that we came to a check-point and we would be turned away as usual, this -- we wanted to see was there a check-point there and where are we going to land. In fact there was no check-point at all. We just continued the journey and found ourselves at the south entry to Mostar, below the heights of Donja Mahala, fairly far in, not too far away from the Old Bridge. And there suddenly fire was opened and I must say that first of all these were warning shots, quite a few, but they were warning shots because the car could easily have been hit. And I don't know from what side it came. It was not -- we couldn't decide. We stopped immediately, we turned around and we drove away. And we were so occupied with ourselves that we didn't care about the positions, and vehicles, and buildings, and soldiers at their posts. We were too busy looking after ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, on this day in what kind of vehicle were you travelling?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a non-armoured vehicle. What's it called? I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did the vehicle -- how --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The English vehicle --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was that a Land Rover, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Land Rover. Yes. I'm sorry. Yes. I couldn't remember the name. Land Rover. It was an unarmed Land Rover. And I'm saying it was unarmed in particular because in this area we did have an armoured Land Rover, but this was unarmoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How was this Land Rover painted?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was painted white, and it had the ECMM insignia on top on the hood and on the side. It was clearly recognisable as an ECMM vehicle. And the flag as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to Exhibit 2619. Exhibit 2619.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is a document, an ECMM report, to RC Zenica, and it is dated the 3rd of June, 1993. First of all, this report, would you have seen such a report or this report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that I had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Under paragraph 7 we see: "People met," and the very first one relates to Colonel -- the "HVO 1 Brigade commander - Colonel Obradovic." Is this the same Colonel Obradovic we were referring to or talking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, is sir, if we can look on the second page of this document. The second line from the top, it says: "1st Brigade is involved in only a limited way in the conflict in Mostar." And then the comment is: "Information from Colonel Obradovic suggests strongly a tie between the HVO and the Serbs in this conflict." Were you aware of any such contacts?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, we hadn't been told anything concrete about such contacts. It was at a time -- no. That was something else. I'm sorry. I was thinking of something else. No. We were not informed further about such contacts. I don't know anything more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the next paragraph down from that: "Colonel Obradovic comes across as a strong advocate of military force." And: "He does not believe that the negotiations will solve the conflict in Mostar." Can you add anything to that or do you have any specific knowledge on Colonel Obradovic in this regard?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything in particular about his person, but the -- I received the entry. I didn't meet him myself, and I know he was a very -- very military man, and this is how he spoke, and he dealt accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the -- in my learned colleague could just either read the rest of the paragraph or walk the witness through the rest of the paragraph, because cherry-picking, as it were, is not appropriate in this instance, because if you read the rest of the paragraph it gives context, and I think the context is something that the Prosecution at times, perhaps because they have lack of time, you know, they seem to omit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, further on in this paragraph, it does say that Colonel Obradovic, referring to Colonel Obradovic: "He does not feel that the Vance-Owen Plan will be implemented in the area either as the opposing armies will not be able to work together." Do you have any knowledge of that or can you comment on that? Whether it's accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, this was the beginning of June, the Vance-Owen Plan, in spite of negotiations at a very high level, or the beginning of June, persons had been proposed for the VOP, basically it was common knowledge that this would not have any success. The resistance we noted was strong, but they were strong in -- particularly from the armija, less so on the Croatian side. Obviously, province 10 could have lived with that, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the next part: "When the subject of detainees and prisoners of war was discussed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The rest -- the rest of the paragraph. Don't skip over the vital part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think that the witness has responded to this, and it's clear what the extent of his knowledge is on this paragraph. I can ask the last sentence, but this is something that may be something which can be appropriately be dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The final part that I did want to ask, sir, is just: "M3 will be given access to the Capljina camp tomorrow. This is for prisoners of war." My simple question is do you know whether, after this date of this document, which is the 3rd of June, 1993, whether access was gained to the Capljina camp?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no access to the camp in Capljina. And if you allow me, I'd like to make a brief comment, because this came up in other contexts. In principle, in terms of the working meeting of the international team of Zagreb, we had instructions not in a particular way, and I emphasise this, to concern ourselves with prisons because this was a matter to be dealt with by the International Red Cross. So when we came up against anything or saw anything which we knew to be worthy of report, we informed the Red Cross, but we didn't make any conscious efforts to enter any of these premises. That was not our job. It was -- the International Red Cross was particularly protected here, and we were not, in spite of the diplomatic passes we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, can we turn very quickly to Exhibit 3640. Exhibit 3640.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is, on the face of it, an ECMM report, daily report for 21 July 1993, and at the end the names of Brad and Peter. This document, would you have seen it or know of it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there's only one aspect in this document that I wish to refer to you -- refer you to, and it's in paragraph 3, "Military activity." And the second paragraph dealing with Colonel Obradovic: " ... Confirmed the details of the last attack." If we can just very briefly turn to the third paragraph, and this ties in with what you had said, that Colonel Obradovic was a military man. "Currently the confrontation line is back to the original position." Do you have that? The third paragraph of that section.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "The HVO claim to be prepared for an all-out attack on Mostar including tanks and artillery. They do not have the authorisation for the attack yet ..." My simple question is you as a military man, can you comment on what this means or implies from the point of view of Colonel Obradovic then?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very complex and shows different aspects. The wording which says that they're also prepared against attacks of artillery and tanks is very difficult to find out where they were supposed to come from. They didn't -- weren't there. Maybe from the Serbian side. But whether that was possible, I really want to doubt, put into question. The other thing, authorisation for counter-attack did not exist, and if there was such a counter-attack, there would be civilian victims, civilian casualties. That might mean that with a counter-attack you might not only use handguns but also other weapons, artillery or mortar that would mainly affect the civilian population, not by handguns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we can step off --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything else. If you want me to, then please ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, our time is nearly up, and I wish to deal with only one further aspect, and that is, sir, did you at any stage talk to anybody from a German government organisation called THW?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have talked to members of the THW, also in Medjugorje where they had their base. Also in Mostar, but in Mostar it was only brief. I talked to them in both places, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was the THW?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The THW is a German organisation, a help organisation, also to give support in terms of water supplies, electricity. Not to install electricity but to install lines, and also to help with evacuation, et cetera. In Mostar, they had the task to get the water supplies from West Mostar to East Mostar because the pipes, the water pipes, were destroyed during the war, and there was a shortage of water in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? [Interpretation] Colonel, could you tell us what the abbreviation THW, what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the German abbreviation for Technisches Hilfswerk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, now you say they had the task to get the water supplies from West Mostar to East Mostar because the pipes were destroyed. Can you tell us your discussion? Did it at all deal with whether this -- this activity was successful or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to interrupt their work because they didn't deem it could be safe enough. I'm almost certain, because the situation in Mostar escalated in June and July, that no water supplies were -- were carried out by the THW. To go back in June 1994, when Hans Koschnik took over in Mostar, then the water supplies did exist for East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, can you recall who you talked to, who the person was from THW that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people, but I can remember a Mr. Bosse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were any particular details of why it was unsafe mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall situation was a risk for them in Mostar because the water supplies were to be carried out at the southern bridge, which in 1992, when there was a conflict with the Serbian side, this bridge had been destroyed, and originally the pipes were situated there, the old pipes, and then the new pipes were supposed to be installed there, too, and it was deemed to be not safe enough also because there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, my final question to you is during your time as a monitor during -- or from the period of April to the end of July 1993, did you at any time meet with Mr. Valentin Coric or Mr. Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not met these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kruger. You've complied with the four hours granted to you, because you've used up exactly four hours. We're going to have a 20-minute break, resume at 5 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we're going to move into private session just for a matter after few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to bring the witness in. I seem to understand that this is the Stojic Defence who is going to start for one hour and 50 [as interpreted] minutes, unless they've been given time, extra time, by other teams. We have six documents, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said one hour and 15 minutes, not one and 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I was just looking at the transcript myself, and I noted that the time was wrong. Yes, we shall be using one hour, 15 minutes. We have prepared for the cross-examination. We've prepared for it yesterday. Your binder has six documents, but I think I'll only be using three of those documents during my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. My name is Senka Nozica, and together with Mr. Peter Murphy I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. Yesterday during your testimony you said that you didn't have access to Mostar from the 30th of June, 1993, until the end of your stay on the 24th of July, 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not on the west side, on the east side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said that on the 3rd of July, 1993, precisely because of this possibility of approaching East Mostar or not, you sent a letter of protest to Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If you still have the Prosecution binder in front of you, take a look at that, please. If not, may you be provided with that binder because I want us to look at the letter of protest once again. And the number of document, I'm referring to the Prosecution binder, the number of the document is P 03162.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3162. Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that letter you suggest to Mr. Bruno Stojic, and that is to be found round about the second paragraph, I believe, that if he thinks that your safety and security is jeopardised that he should take the necessary measures and meet you in a safe place. Is that right? Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you met Mr. Stojic in Siroki Brijeg, did you not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a later point in time. I think this was the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Now, in this letter you also say that you know that the BH army attacked the HVO on the 30th of June, 1993, and that you would like information about that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you said that the meeting was convened and held two days later, which would make it the 5th of July, 1993. Would you now take a look -- yes. Thank you. Yes. Would you now take a look at this document again. P 03196 is the number.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to a question from my learned colleague of the Prosecution you explained the first part of the document under number 2, the political situation or political activity, and you told us what you discussed with Mr. Stojic. Now, I would like us to take a look at section number 3, which relates to military activities. And in that passage you take note of the fact that Mr. Bruno Stojic gave comments with respect to the military situation. And first of all, he said that the BH army had taken control of the barracks in North Mostar, and then he said that during the combat activities in Bijelo Polje many people were murdered and taken prisoner. Now, did you have information that on that same occasion the BH army took control of the broader area in the northern part of Mostar in addition to the place mentioned, which was Bijelo Polje, and the Potok and Rastani settlements, and that the Croatian population, which was the majority population in these places, were either taken prisoner or expelled to West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The extent of the area we didn't know so precisely. We could only say in general terms. As far as the Croatic population is concerned, we didn't know that either by the nature of things, but sometime later I talked to a mother and a daughter. I conducted an interview in Siroki Brijeg, who had come on the way from this camp to Siroki Brijeg, and I heard the details from them what happened, that is, from the point of view of this mother and daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that the mother and daughter came from the area that we're discussing, that is to say, west of Mostar, from that area? That's where they came from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly this is a misunderstanding. I mean the area to the east of the Neretva. I'm not sure about the names of the places, but east of the Neretva at the north of Mostar. Rastani is one place, but as I say, I'm not sure of the names of places. I would have to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's precisely what I asked you. Now, following on this report you say that Mr. Stojic told you that the BH army wished to attack the entire area of Bugojno, Jablanica, in order to reach the Adriatic coast after that. So I'm talking about -- well, you said Bugojno, Prozor, Jablanica, Mostar, with a view to emerging on the Adriatic coast. Now, do you know that later on while you were still in the area some of these military activities did actually place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact the essential activities in -- well, in Jablanica, Konjic, and the lake and north of that towards Breznice, at that time they were over, so this would have been new attacks. May I add something to that? These towns in the north would indicate that it has nothing to do with the Adriatic coast, but what we mean is that if there was an attack to the south then considerable forces would have to be brought in from the north. Otherwise, this would not be possible. This is how it is meant to be understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that later on, the Bugojno situation, because Bugojno and the attack by the BH army on Bugojno was something that was mentioned several times in your reports, especially the reports that were shown to you over the past two days by the Prosecutor. Now, what I want to ask you is this: Do you know whether Mr. Stojic -- well, Mr. Stojic went on to tell you that over the next three days the BH army would attack Mostar from three directions. And then what is mentioned here is Rastani, the centre of town, and from the direction of Buna. Now, do you know whether the BH army did indeed attack the HVO from those axes at that time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know that, because at the time we had no access more, at least to East Mostar. And basically this was one of the reasons to check this or not; we wanted to know what was happening with the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. In your reports there is some information about this, and we'll go on to clarify that a little later on. But let us now take a look at your assessments. You make your assessments at the end of the report. You said that the report was compiled together with your colleague, and I'd like to read through this passage very slowly, and then I'd like to ask you for some comments. In the second paragraph, you say: "In this complicated situation in which the Croats are fighting the Muslims, and sometimes also still with the Serbs ..." I'd like to stop there for a moment. And tell me on that 5th of July what information you had in order to be able to say that the Croats were still engaged in warfare against the Serbs, that they were still fighting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, these were individual statements by HVO soldiers that again and again there were artillery attacks from the Serbian side but fewer conflicts with infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you go on to say that it was a conflict in which the BH army had gained some military successes and during which there was mobilisation, and there was certain restrictions being implemented in civilian life, and within the frameworks of the HVO there were conflicts and arguments going on, and there was the problem of Croatian and Muslim refugees and a mutiny of the Muslim soldiers. And on the other hand, their arrests, the enormous inflation rate that had to be contended with, combined with economic difficulties, and then you say: "The Croatian leadership may feel that the difficulties arise from within the population, which it is difficult for them to control. So this went very far. And we cannot think that the Croats just exaggerated and that they were playing a game with international agencies. The question, however, remains is how credible they are." So this is an assessment made on your part. I won't go into the details, but I'd just like to know whether this was your assessment on the basis of your experience gained in the area from your arrival there until the 5th of September when this report was compiled.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, basically, these are my own experiences and those of the other monitors, and these resulted from discussions with the former leaders of the HCC in Zenica, but these were accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Ms. Nozica, you will wish to correct the transcript where on page 39, it is spoken of September rather than July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just looking at that. Thank you. Perhaps I misspoke. If I did, it was a slip of the tongue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the period before this meeting, because in the statement you gave on the 18th and 19th of February to the OTP, 1998, you provided a lot of information about what was going on in April 1993, in the broader area around Jablanica, Konjic, and the area north of Mostar in general. I'd just like to remind you of some of the events that you referred to in your statement, and you have direct knowledge of those, of course. You stayed in your statement that the first major conflict between the HVO and the BH army started on the 8th of April, 1993, in the area of Klis in the village of Seonica. You went there. You saw what was going on. You saw the school in which the HVO was located and it was targeted with a number of artillery pieces. So I'd just like to ask you briefly to tell us what you remember from that visit or of the event itself.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our accommodation in Siroki Brijeg, early in the morning we were called by the office of the minister of defence. From the office, not from him personally. In Seonica there were conflicts as you described, and we should look into it. Then a monitor and myself and an interpreter went to Seonica and the following happened: We went into the town, the left-hand side. We saw the school building you mentioned. There were two HVO soldiers, platoon commanders about this rank, and Rabenstein was one name that I remember, and they showed us the inside of the school, the outside of the school, the school -- the windows were broken. There were many impacts in the walls by infantry munition, and in the school, through the windows we saw that the furniture was all over the place. You could see impacts all over the school building. There were very many of them. More than a hundred perhaps, but a great deal. It wasn't artillery, as you said, but according to the indications and we could assume from what we saw that these had -- were the result of machine-gun fire. There was a position indicated about a hundred metres away from the school. Then we continued in the village about a hundred, 200 metres, approximately, and we came into the Muslim part of the village. The previous part was the part of the Croatian population. And then we met with local leaders. We came across local leaders, and we said to them, "What is happening?" And it's been alleged that people have shot in the school. And they didn't contest this, but they took us to the mosque, and they said that mortar grenade -- a shell had been fired at the mosque and here are the remnants of the mortar shell. Let me add, I remember this so well because shortly after my return I used this terrible episode in my presentations to give an impression, after I got back to Germany. Otherwise, I wouldn't remember these details. Then we looked at the mortar shells. They were old mortar shells. There were signs of rust. It was certainly not the mortar shells that had made the hole in the mosque, which was in fact there. At the top, on the top of the roof there was a hole. Then we went to about the middle of the village. There was a small square. We were there with interpreters and met with both sides, and we had a lengthy conversation with both sides and called upon them to establish order and peace, and this was said to take several days. How long it took, we don't know. And then we continued our journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the interpretation to finish. Yes. That's precisely what you said in very precise terms in your statement, what you noticed, that next to the mosque you were shown this mortar, but that you observed that the mortar was an old one and that it couldn't have been used in that particular conflict. Now, in June you visited the village of Vucjak. Were you told what happened in that village on the 14th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vucjak. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There's Vucjak, but it is Buscak, with a B, B-u-s.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To say it again, it's a place above the command post of the armija corps of the brigade. So it's one of the main roads going to Klis. I can't recall the name. It's above 10 kilometres. Is it Pazavic? Does it exist? Pazaric, or something like that? So above this place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this incident on the 8th of April, a few days later we were called again by the ministry of Mr. Stojic in Mostar, and then we talked with the deputy Prime Minister there. We, I meant the other monitor, Kiki Salamanca. And Mr. Bozic told us of several places where some attacks were made against the Croat population. And then at a later point in time, I can't remember exactly -- the exact date, I went again there again, and then I heard the following from several people, and several of them spoke German because several worked as guest workers near Stuttgart, not all with interpretation. And I think they said on the 14th of June, at night, masked men penetrated buildings which were inhabited by Croats, and in one or two buildings they shot dead one of the husbands and her brother. We talked to the woman. And in the other building a neighbour. But I think this visit took place in Buscak in the middle of June. The woman also showed us the room which was in a bad state. You could see impacts on the floor. Obviously, fighting had been going on. Then some other people confirmed this, that they had been robbed. Money was taken. Cars had been stolen. They also said that some Croats had moved from the area or had migrated elsewhere, if I can put like that, but she stayed behind, she said, with her children because she didn't know what else to do. And at night, so she said, she also -- she always spent the night with a Muslim neighbour in order to feel safe. So despite what you heard from other places, the -- the neighbourhood between Croats and Muslims did work out fine. So this was the result of our visit. Again, we made a report to the International Red Cross and to the other international groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I may, sir, you spoke about the 14th of June. If I may just remind you, I assume that when you made your statement on the 18th and the 19th of February, 1998, you remembered all these things more clearly than now. If you could please set me right about some dates. Here you say, "In June, I visited the village of Buscak in the surroundings of Klis where a Croat lady told me that on the evening of the 14th of April, in her home, three of their own men had been killed. There are official reports to show that this indeed occurred on the 14th of April." So if I could please ask you to try to think back and remember as best you can, because this is something that you mentioned in your answer as having occurred in June.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been a misunderstanding, because my visit was in June. It was two months later. Indeed, the woman did say clearly -- whether it was on the 14th I can't quite tell, but the date was clearly in the middle of April. I think it was the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have very little time for this cross, and I will be dropping some of the events in April which you have already described, but there is something that you said that I wish to point out to you now to see whether you can confirm that. In your statement you say, "In late April, little by little we got the impression that the Muslims were trying to expel the Croats from the southern part of Central Bosnia." Do you remember saying this, sir, and could you still confirm this statement, this assertion as it is today? We are talking about what, sir, went on in April.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this. This was also confirmed by other organisations. I can also confirm it using an example, that is Konjic, the expulsion of the priests there. I don't know how long they actually stayed there. They were threatened, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed we have been mentioning Konjic quite often, haven't we, but what I had in mind was the entire region, and that's why your statement applies. I asked you earlier today, in connection with your conversation with Mr. Stojic on the 5th of July, 1993, whether you knew about these events that later took place in Bugojno. If you could please use the binder provided by the Prosecution, please, the document number is P 03611.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have got the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is dated the 21st of July, 1993. On page 1 we have this. This is in relation to the fighting in Bugojno. It says the expected cease-fire has not taken effect in Bugojno because the BH side refused to accept it. Let me ask you first. Can you remember that on or around the 18th of July, 1993, an attack by the BH army in Bugojno commenced, which for the most part had been completed by the end of your own mandate? Do you remember this, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that because Bugojno is well outside of our area of responsibility, and I only know Bugojno from driving through, that's all. But I was surprised when, at the end of July, I went to Zenica with Sir Martin Garrod, as I already mentioned. Then we went through Bugojno, and I was surprised about the level of destruction of the houses. And also when we talked to people, they said that parts of the church had been destroyed as well. But I was surprised about the level of destruction. But then I don't know the place personally, and again I'm -- everything was being referred to that had been reports that had been compiled by other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What you say about mid-July, are you talking about Zenica or about Bugojno? I'm not sure I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Bugojno, because when I went to Zenica, I went through Bugojno for the first time, because otherwise I'd never been there. On the way to Zenica, and then I saw the level of destruction in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Indeed. Back to the report that we're looking at. I assume that you have seen it before, because the -- you answered a number of questions from the OTP in relation to this document.
